gaps.reason: No official source I read says whether the MSP Central Records Division releases crash reports written by county, municipal or sheriff agencies, or only MSP's own. MDSP calls the division the state's 'central repository', but COMAR 29.02.02.01(C) refers to 'State Police investigated accident reports', and the online form expects case numbers in the 'YYMSP######' format. The MDTA Police Central Records page, which a search snippet said lacks access to other agencies' reports, returned HTTP 403 and was not read or used.

There is no single official statewide instruction for crashes handled by county police or sheriffs. Only the Baltimore City referral (on the MDSP page) and Montgomery County's own process were confirmed. Readers should contact the agency that responded. Other counties' procedures and fees were not checked.

Official sources conflict. MDSP's current page says to wait at least 10 days. COMAR 29.02.02.01(B) still says requests won't be considered until at least 20 days after the crash. The online form asks for 10 business days to respond. No official source gives a typical total turnaround for a mailed request.

No card, convenience or online fee applies to MSP reports; payment is by check or money order only. The BuyCrash price for Baltimore City reports was not confirmed on an official or vendor page, and Baltimore Police's own fee was not stated on the page read.

MDSP says it releases reports to 'legally entitled parties' under MDSP policy and the Public Information Act, but does not define who qualifies. Apart from the attorney-solicitation bar in General Provisions § 4-315, I found no statewide involved-parties-only rule or confidentiality period. Montgomery County's involved-party check is a county practice.

The statute requires a written report to 'the Administration' within 15 days for injury or fatal crashes. The Motor Vehicle Administration's own page, with the form name, number and how to file it, could not be read: mva.maryland.gov returned HTTP 403. The web search budget ran out before another official source could be found.

MSP has no fully online purchase. The Google Form starts the request, but the $4 must still be paid by check or money order. MSP's request email address is obfuscated on the MDSP page and was confirmed only in the online form's contact text.

facts.claim: The Maine State Police run an online service for searching and requesting crash reports from the Maine State Police Crash Database.
facts.quote: Search and request crash reports online from the Maine State Police Crash Database.

facts.claim: The crash ordering service is run by the Maine Department of Public Safety, Maine State Police.
facts.quote: A secure, online service provided by the Department of Public Safety - Maine State Police

facts.claim: The investigating officer completes the crash report and sends it to the Maine State Police Traffic Division.
facts.quote: The Crash report is the report the investigating officer completes and sends to the Maine State Police, Traffic Division.

facts.claim: Under Maine law, the Chief of the State Police must receive, tabulate and analyze accident reports.
facts.quote: Shall receive, tabulate and analyze accident reports;

facts.claim: Under Maine law, the Chief of the State Police must send all accident reports to the Secretary of State.
facts.quote: Shall send all accident reports to the Secretary of State; and

facts.claim: The Maine State Police media resources page links to Maine Crash Reporting as the site for searching Maine crash reports and says fees apply.
facts.quote: This is a site where you can search Maine Crash reports. Fees apply.

facts.claim: The statute's duties to investigate and report apply to any law enforcement officer who investigates a reportable accident.
facts.quote: A law enforcement officer who investigates a reportable accident shall:

facts.claim: A 2010 Maine State Police crash reporting manual says that since the Maine Crash Reporting System started in 2003, Maine has collected all crash data from investigating police departments electronically.
facts.quote: In 2003, with the implementation of the Maine Crash Reporting System (MCRS), Maine became the first state in the Nation to collect all crash data from investigating police departments electronically with no data entry.

facts.claim: The state portal can be searched by name, date of birth, crash location, crash date or investigating police department.
facts.quote: You can search by name, date of birth, crash location, crash date, or investigating agency (police department).

facts.claim: The state portal's search form lists county sheriffs' offices and municipal police departments as investigating agencies you can search by.
facts.quote: Washington County Sheriffs Dept Waterville Police Department Wells Police Department Westbrook Police Department

facts.claim: According to the state FAQ, non-reportable crashes (under $1000 combined damage with no injury reported at the scene) are not kept in the state system.
facts.quote: If your crash was less than $1000 combined damage, and no personal injury was reported at the scene, then your crash was NON-REPORTABLE. Non-reportable crashes are not maintained in this system.

facts.claim: ATV or snowmobile crashes covered by the Maine Warden Service are not in the state crash database, so you need to contact the Maine Warden Service.
facts.quote: If your crash involved an ATV or snowmobile and was covered by the Maine Warden Service the crash will not be in our database. You will need to contact the Maine Warden Service at (207) 287-2766.

facts.claim: Not every crash was in the state database until January 1, 2003.
facts.quote: Not all crashes were available in the database until January 1, 2003.

facts.claim: Crash records from 1976 through 2002 are on microfilm and are available by written request with payment to the Maine State Police Traffic Division in Augusta.
facts.quote: 1976 thru 2002 are on microfilm and are available by making a written request with payment to the Maine State Police, Traffic Division, State House Station #20, Augusta, Maine 04333-0020.

facts.claim: If the online search finds matching reports, you can request one or more and pay by credit card or with an InforME subscription.
facts.quote: If reports are found matching your search criteria, you will have the option to request one or more, with a credit card payment or subscription to InforME.

facts.claim: Reports ordered online are sent by email.
facts.quote: The report(s) will be sent to you via email.

facts.claim: If you have no email, you can ask for the report to be faxed, though email is preferred.
facts.quote: If you do not have email capability at the time your crash report is found you can request the report be sent via fax. It is preferable that you utilize email if possible.

facts.claim: You can buy your report online or mail the request form from the portal's homepage to the Maine State Police Traffic Division.
facts.quote: You may search for your report and purchase it online, or use the request form from the homepage to mail to the Maine State Police Traffic Division.

facts.claim: For a manual search you can pay online or by check, and paying by check means downloading, printing and completing the linked request form.
facts.quote: You may pay online or pay by check. To send a payment by check to the Maine State Police Traffic Division, please download, print and complete this form

facts.claim: For crashes before January 1, 2003, you can print a crash request form and send it with payment to the Maine State Police Traffic Division, State House Station #20, Augusta, Maine 04333-0020.
facts.quote: You can print a crash request form for pre January 1, 2003 crashes from the web page and send it with payment to the Maine State Police, Traffic Division, State House Station #20, Augusta, Maine 04333-0020.

facts.claim: The mail-in request form (revised 9/1/2005) says checks should be made payable to Treasurer State of Maine.
facts.quote: Make check payable to: Treasurer State of Maine

facts.claim: The mail-in request form asks you to enclose a self-addressed envelope.
facts.quote: PLEASE ENCLOSE A SELF-ADDRESSED ENVELOPE

facts.claim: If no match is found for a crash before 2003, you must submit a manual search request to the Maine State Police Traffic Division.
facts.quote: If no match is found for a pre-2003 crash, you need to submit a request the Maine State Police Traffic Division for a manual search.

facts.claim: A report found through a manual search is sent by regular mail, fax or email, and you get an email about the search status within 7 business days if you give an email address.
facts.quote: If your crash report is found it will be sent to you via regular mail, fax or email. This fee is non-refundable. You will receive an email regarding the status of your search within 7 business days if your email address is submitted.

facts.claim: To pay for a hand search by credit or debit card, you can email the Maine State Police Traffic Division with the information it needs.
facts.quote: If you would like to pay via credit card/debit card to InforMe you may click the email link to Maine State Police Traffic Division and provide the requested information necessary for us to perform a hand search of the crash.

facts.claim: Maine law says that on written request the Chief of the State Police may provide a photocopy of the investigating officer's report at the requester's expense.
facts.quote: On written request, the chief may furnish a photocopy of the investigating officer's report at the expense of the person making the request.

facts.claim: To use the online service you need the name and date of birth of someone on the crash report.
facts.quote: The name & date of birth of an individual on the crash report

facts.claim: To order online you need a Mastercard, Visa or Discover credit card or an InforME subscription.
facts.quote: A credit card (Mastercard, Visa or Discover) or subscription with InforME (for orders only)

facts.claim: You need Adobe Reader to view or print the crash report, which is a PDF.
facts.quote: You will need Adobe Reader to view or print a crash report (PDF).

facts.claim: The person you search for can be a driver, a passenger, a pedestrian or a witness, and you can also search by crash location, crash date or investigating police department.
facts.quote: This individual may be the operator of a vehicle, a passenger in the vehicle, a pedestrian, or a witness. You may also search by crash location, crash date, or by investigating police department.

facts.claim: The online search form accepts a Crash Incident ID Number if you have one.
facts.quote: CRASH INCIDENT ID NUMBER: (If available, please indicate only Crash Incident ID Number).

facts.claim: To search by name, you enter the person's first name, last name and date of birth.
facts.quote: To search by name, you should enter a first name, last name, and date of birth for the individual in the crash.

facts.claim: The easiest searches usually use the crash date with the town, or the crash date with a last name.
facts.quote: In most cases the easiest searches are performed by providing the following information: Date of crash and town crash occurred in, or Date of crash and last name

facts.claim: Some agencies give people involved in a crash a printed driver's report form at the scene, which has the information needed to search for the crash report.
facts.quote: Some agencies will supply persons involved in a crash a printed "driver's report form" at the scene. This document provides all the necessary information for searching a crash report.

facts.claim: A manual search needs the name and date of birth of an operator in the crash, plus the crash date or location, and your contact information.
facts.quote: For a manual search, you must provide the name and the date of birth of an operator involved in the crash, plus either the date or the location of the crash. Your contact information is also required.

facts.claim: The mail-in request form asks for the legal name, date of birth and residence of the operators involved.
facts.quote: Legal Name, Date of Birth and Residence of involved OPERATORS:

facts.claim: Each crash report ordered through the state online service costs $10.00.
facts.quote: Each report costs $10.00.

facts.claim: You are not charged if your search finds no matches.
facts.quote: If no matches are found for your search, you will not be charged.

facts.claim: A manual search request costs $10.00, and the fee is non-refundable.
facts.quote: The fee to submit a manual search is $10.00, this fee is non refundable.

facts.claim: The mail-in request form lists the Police Traffic Crash Report at $10.00.
facts.quote: Police Traffic Crash Report-$10.00

facts.claim: The mail-in request form lists an Officers Investigative Report at $10.00, available only for fatal crashes investigated by the Maine State Police.
facts.quote: Officers Investigative Report-$10.00 FOR FATALS INVESTIGATED BY MAINE STATE POLICE ONLY!

facts.claim: Maine law says the cost of a copy of the investigating officer's report is not subject to the limits in Title 1, section 408-A, the state's public-records fee limits.
facts.quote: On written request, the chief may furnish a photocopy of the investigating officer's report at the expense of the person making the request. The cost of furnishing a copy of the report is not subject to the limitations of Title 1, section 408

facts.claim: Most reports ordered online are sent within two hours of the order.
facts.quote: Most reports will be sent within two hours of your order.

facts.claim: If your crash details are correct and the report is in the database, you should get it within 24 hours of the search.
facts.quote: If the information you provide regarding the crash is correct and the report is in the database you should receive the crash report within 24 hours of the search.

facts.claim: If a report is not found, the investigating agency may not have submitted it yet, so you should try again in a few days because reports are downloaded daily.
facts.quote: The investigating agency may not have submitted the crash report to the Maine State Police Traffic Division. Try again in a few days. Reports are downloaded daily.

facts.claim: Maine law requires the investigating officer to send the report to the Chief of the State Police within 5 days of being notified of the accident.
facts.quote: Within 5 days from the time of notification of the accident, transmit an electronic report or the original written report containing all available information to the Chief of the State Police.

facts.claim: If your details are correct and the report is on microfilm, you may get it in five days or less.
facts.quote: If the information you provide is correct and the crash report is in our microfilm database you may receive the crash report in five days or less.

facts.claim: The state FAQ says anyone who wants to buy a crash report can do so.
facts.quote: Anyone who would like to purchase the report can do so.

facts.claim: Maine law lets the Chief of the State Police disclose an accident's date, time and location and the names and addresses of operators, owners, injured persons, witnesses and the investigating officer.
facts.quote: the Chief of the State Police may disclose the date, time and location of the accident and the names and addresses of operators, owners, injured persons, witnesses and the investigating officer.

facts.claim: The state crash report may not be the whole file: the investigating agency may hold more reports, such as officer narratives, witness statements, photographs or other recordings.
facts.quote: there may be additional reports pertaining to this incident on file with the investigating law enforcement agency. These reports may include officer narratives, witness statements, photographs or other recordings.

facts.claim: For those additional reports, you contact the investigating agency directly.
facts.quote: You should contact the investigating agency directly to inquire about the existence and availability of these reports.

facts.claim: For a non-reportable crash, contact the department called to the scene, which should have an incident report on file.
facts.quote: Please contact the department called to the scene. An incident report should be on file at that office.

facts.claim: The driver information from a crash may be printed at the scene, or you can get it later from the investigating agency.
facts.quote: They may be able to print this at the scene or at a later time you should be able to get it from the investigating agency.

facts.claim: The City of Waterville's police page says the department partners with BuyCrash to provide online access to Waterville crash reports.
facts.quote: As a service to our residents and the business community, Waterville Police Department is proud to announce a partnership with BuyCrash to provide online access to all Waterville Maine crash reports.

facts.claim: Waterville says its crash reports are available 48 hours after the crash, or sooner if completed, except fatal crashes and crashes under investigation, and fatal crash reports must be bought at the Waterville Police Department.
facts.quote: All crash reports will be available 48 hours after the crash occurs (or sooner if completed) except for fatal crashes and crashes under investigation. Fatal crash reports must be purchased at the Waterville Police Department.

facts.claim: Waterville's page says BuyCrash.com has both reportable and non-reportable crash reports within one hour of report completion.
facts.quote: BuyCrash.com provides access to both reportable and non-reportable crash reports within one hour of report completion.

facts.claim: The City of South Portland's police page says the department partners with BuyCrash.com to provide online access to South Portland crash reports.
facts.quote: South Portland Police Department is proud to announce a partnership with BuyCrash.com to provide online access to all South Portland Maine crash reports.

facts.claim: South Portland says its crash reports are available 72 hours after the crash, or sooner if completed, except fatal crashes and crashes under investigation, and fatal crash reports must be bought at the South Portland Police Department.
facts.quote: All crash reports will be available 72 hours after the crash occurs (or sooner if completed) except for fatal crashes and crashes under investigation. Fatal crash reports must be purchased at the South Portland Police Department.

facts.claim: Maine law defines a reportable accident as one on a public way or place where public traffic is expected that causes bodily injury, death or apparent property damage of $2,000 or more.
facts.quote: As used in this section, "reportable accident" means an accident on a public way or a place where public traffic may reasonably be anticipated, resulting in bodily injury or death to a person or apparent property damage of $2,000 or more.

facts.claim: A reportable accident must be reported immediately, by the quickest means, to a state police officer, the nearest state police field office, the sheriff's office or a deputy sheriff in the county where it happened.
facts.quote: A reportable accident must be reported immediately by the quickest means of communication to a state police officer, or to the nearest state police field office, or to the sheriff's office, or to a deputy sheriff, within the county in which the accident occurred

facts.claim: The report can also be made to the police department, or an officer, of the municipality where the accident happened.
facts.quote: or to the office of the police department, or to an officer, of the municipality in which the accident occurred.

facts.claim: The operator of an involved vehicle is the first person the law names as responsible for reporting the accident.
facts.quote: The accident must be reported by: A. The operator of an involved vehicle;

facts.claim: Section 2251's former subsection 5, the forty-eight-hour report, is marked repealed (RP) by PL 2003, c. 434.
facts.quote: Forty-eight-hour report. [PL 2003, c. 434, §25 (RP); PL 2003, c. 434, §37 (AFF).]

facts.claim: The owner or operator of a vehicle in an accident must give the Secretary of State any additional information it requires to decide whether proof of financial responsibility applies.
facts.quote: The owner or operator of a vehicle involved in an accident shall furnish additional relevant information as the Secretary of State requires to determine the applicability of the requirement of proof of financial responsibility.

facts.claim: Knowingly failing to make a required oral or written report within the time required is a Class E crime.
facts.quote: A person commits a Class E crime if that person: A. Is required to make an oral or written report and knowingly fails to do so within the time required;

facts.claim: Only the investigating officer can change a crash report, so corrections go to that officer.
facts.quote: No. You must contact the investigating officer. The officer is the only person who can make changes to the report.

facts.claim: Maine law says statements in the accident report may not be admitted as evidence in any civil or criminal trial arising out of the accident.
facts.quote: may not be admitted in evidence in any trial, civil or criminal, arising out of the accident.

facts.claim: The Maine State Police Investigative Records unit says police investigative and intelligence records are not generally public records in Maine, and their release is restricted under Title 16, chapter 9.
facts.quote: Please be advised that police investigative and intelligence records are not generally considered public records under Maine law, and the release of such records is restricted under Title 16, chapter 9 of the Maine Revised Statutes Annotated.

gaps.reason: No convenience or card-processing fee is stated on the pages read. Only the $10.00 per-report and $10.00 manual-search fees are listed. Any card fee would appear at checkout, which was not reached because this was read-only research.

The thresholds conflict. The state crash-service FAQ defines a reportable crash as $1000.00 or more in apparent damage (or any injury or death), but 29-A M.R.S. §2251(1), amended by PL 2023, c. 27, now says $2,000 or more. The FAQ appears not to have been updated. Use the statutory $2,000 figure for the legal definition, and note that the FAQ still uses $1000 to explain which crashes are in the system.

The state FAQ says anyone may buy a report, but §2251(7-A)(B) bars the Bureau of State Police from publicly disseminating personally identifying accident report data in its database (with listed exceptions). No official page read explains how the two fit together. No requester-eligibility rule, involved-party limit or waiting period was found.

The only mail-in form found is marked 'revised 9/1/ 2005'. The current pages link it for paying by check on manual searches, and the FAQ points to it for pre-2003 crashes. It also lists 2005-era fees for reconstruction, vehicle autopsy and forensic mapping, which may be superseded by the 2021 DPS Uniform Public Records Request Fee Schedule. Only its $10.00 crash-report fee is reported here.
No official source found describes requesting a crash report in person from the Maine State Police Traffic Division.

The Traffic Division phone number differs across official pages: (207) 624-8944 on the portal homepage, search form and mail form, and (207) 624-8939 on the apps1 FAQ and the 2010 manual. Email mcrs_response@maine.gov is the same on every page.

No official state source gives a typical number of days from crash to availability in the online database. The sources say only that officers must submit within 5 days of notification, that reports are downloaded daily, and that a requester should 'try again in a few days'. The 48- and 72-hour figures come from individual city pages (Waterville, South Portland) and apply only to those departments.

No official source names a driver-filed crash report form for a state agency. The statute requires reporting immediately to police, and the old 'Forty-eight-hour report' subsection is repealed. The Secretary of State may ask for financial-responsibility information, but no form name or deadline for that was found.

No statewide official list shows which local police departments or sheriffs sell reports through BuyCrash or another vendor, or what local agencies charge. Only the Waterville and South Portland city pages were confirmed. Readers should ask the investigating agency directly.

The 'collects all crash data from investigating police departments' statement comes from a Maine State Police manual revised August 2010. No newer official statement on coverage was found, though the live search form lists municipal police departments and county sheriffs as investigating agencies.

facts.claim: The Michigan State Police Traffic Crash Reporting Unit maintains the Traffic Crash Reporting System (TCRS) database, the central repository for all traffic crash data for the State of Michigan.
facts.quote: The Unit maintains the Traffic Crash Reporting System (TCRS) database that serves as the central repository for all traffic crash data for the State of Michigan.

facts.claim: The State of Michigan Traffic Crash Report (UD-10) must by law (MCL 257.622) be completed on all reportable crashes.
facts.quote: The State of Michigan Traffic Crash Report (UD-10) is a form that must be completed by law (Michigan Compiled Law [MCL].257.622) on all reportable crashes.

facts.claim: All law enforcement agencies complete the UD-10 report and forward it to the Michigan State Police.
facts.quote: The report is completed by all law enforcement agencies and is forwarded to the Michigan State Police for analysis for the purpose of furnishing statistical information and preparing compiled crash data.

facts.claim: The Traffic Crash Purchasing System sells traffic crash reports submitted by all Michigan law enforcement agencies.
facts.quote: The Traffic Crash Purchasing System allows individuals to purchase traffic crash reports submitted by all Michigan law enforcement agencies for a fee of $15.00.

facts.claim: Reports can be purchased through the Traffic Crash Reporting Unit up to 10 years after the crash, and older records must be requested through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request.
facts.quote: You can purchase your report through the Traffic Crash Reporting Unit up to 10 years after the crash occurred. Any records that are outside of that timeframe will need to be requested by submitting a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) Request.

facts.claim: The MSP Traffic Crash Reporting Unit says the UD-10 must be purchased online through the Traffic Crash Purchasing System (TCPS) website and calls this the only way to obtain a traffic crash report.
facts.quote: The Traffic Crash Report (UD-10) must be purchased online. This is the only way to obtain a traffic crash report. Individuals can get a copy of a Michigan Traffic Crash Report by using the Traffic Crash Purchasing System (TCPS) website.

facts.claim: Effective April 14, 2026, the TCPS is accessed through MiLogin.
facts.quote: Effective April 14, 2026, the Michigan State Police transitioned to a Traffic Crash Purchasing System (TCPS) that is accessed through MiLogin.

facts.claim: The previous TCPS site is no longer available because the TCPS has migrated to MiLogin.
facts.quote: Please note that the TCPS has migrated to MiLogin and the previous TCPS site is no longer available for use.

facts.claim: The TCPS site is at www.michigan.gov/tcps, and users must register or log in there before TCPS appears among their MiLogin services.
facts.quote: The Traffic Crash Purchasing System will not appear in your accessible MiLogin services until you have registered/logged into the TCPS site at www.michigan.gov/tcps.

facts.claim: The MSP FOIA FAQ says a copy of a traffic crash report (UD-010) can be obtained instantly through the Traffic Crash Purchasing System (TCPS).
facts.quote: You can obtain a copy of a traffic crash report (UD-010) instantly by utilizing the Traffic Crash Purchasing System (TCPS).

facts.claim: The MSP FOIA FAQ says that instead of the TCPS you can request a crash report through the Public Records Request Portal, or by email, fax or mail.
facts.quote: If you choose not to use the TCPS, you can submit your request via the Public Records Request Portal. If you choose not to use the online portal, you may alternatively submit your request by email, fax, or mail.

facts.claim: MSP public records requests are submitted through the MSP Records Request Portal, which is accessed through MILogin.
facts.quote: For public records from the Michigan State Police (MSP), please submit your request through the MSP Records Request Portal, which can be accessed below through MILogin.

facts.claim: If you need specific information from the UD-10, the MSP says to buy the report through TCPS or submit a FOIA request.
facts.quote: If you need specific information from the Traffic Crash Report (UD-10), you will need to purchase the report through the Traffic Crash Purchasing System (TCPS) or submit a Freedom of Information Act Request (FOIA).

facts.claim: No form is required for an MSP records request, but the DIR-101 Request for Public Records form can be used to help draft one.
facts.quote: No, a form is not required; however, you may use the DIR-101 Request for Public Records form to assist in drafting your request.

facts.claim: Check or money order payments for MSP records requests can be mailed to Michigan State Police, Cashier's Unit, P.O. Box 30266, Lansing, Michigan 48909.
facts.quote: Payments can be mailed to Michigan State Police, Cashier’s Unit, P.O. Box 30266, Lansing, Michigan 48909.

facts.claim: For MSP records requests, documents may be picked up at MSP Headquarters in Dimondale if the Records Resource Section is given advance notice.
facts.quote: If advance notice is provided to the Records Resource Section, documents may be picked up at the MSP Headquarters in Dimondale.

facts.claim: You must register for an account before searching for a report.
facts.quote: All users must register for an account prior to searching for their report.

facts.claim: Accounts created on the previous TCPS website do not transfer, so individuals and businesses must create a new MiLogin account.
facts.quote: Accounts that were created on the previous TCPS website will not transfer. Individuals and Businesses must create a new account in MiLogin.

facts.claim: Get the report incident/case number from the law enforcement agency that reported the crash, or from the MSP post for the county if the Michigan State Police handled it.
facts.quote: Contact the law enforcement agency that is reporting the accident to get the report incident/case number. If it was the Michigan State Police, you will need to contact the Michigan State Police post for the County in which the crash occurred.

facts.claim: A copy of the report costs $15.00.
facts.quote: There is a $15.00 fee to obtain a copy of the report.

facts.claim: TCPS sells crash reports for a fee of $15.00.
facts.quote: The Traffic Crash Purchasing System allows individuals to purchase traffic crash reports submitted by all Michigan law enforcement agencies for a fee of $15.00.

facts.claim: For MSP records requests, the fee varies with the type of record and the labor cost of retrieving and reviewing it.
facts.quote: The fee varies based on the type of record and the labor costs for retrieval and review of the documents.

facts.claim: For MSP records requests, requesters who meet the indigency criteria and submit an Affidavit of Indigency may have the first $20 of the fee waived.
facts.quote: For requestors that meet the indigency criteria, you may submit an Affidavit of Indigency along with your request. If you qualify, the first $20 of the fee will be waived.

facts.claim: It can take 3 - 30 days after the crash for the report to be processed into the TCPS database and become available to buy online.
facts.quote: It can take 3 - 30 days following the crash for the report to be processed into the TCPS database and made available online for purchase.

facts.claim: Law enforcement agencies have no mandatory deadline to submit the UD-10 to the MSP, and the typical processing time of 3 – 30 days depends on the reporting agency.
facts.quote: There is not a mandatory timeframe for which a law enforcement agency needs to submit the complete Traffic Crash Report (UD-10) to the Michigan State Police. The typical processing time is 3 – 30 days, however, this is dependent on the reporting agency.

facts.claim: The MSP responds to a records request within 5 business days, and the response may be a notice of extension.
facts.quote: Once a request has been received, a response will be issued within 5 business days. The response may be a notice of extension allowing the MSP additional time to gather and review the responsive records.

facts.claim: The MSP gives an individual seeking a report on a crash they were involved in as an example of a citizen MiLogin account user of TCPS.
facts.quote: An example of this within the Traffic Crash Purchasing System (TCPS) would be an individual looking for a traffic crash report for an incident that they were involved in.

facts.claim: The MSP gives an insurance company buying multiple reports as an example of a MiLogin for Business account user of TCPS.
facts.quote: An example of this type of account for the Traffic Crash Purchasing System (TCPS) would be an insurance company that needs to purchase multiple reports for their business.

facts.claim: The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit will not release information such as insurance details, report numbers or personal details of those involved, though it can confirm or deny information you already have.
facts.quote: The Unit is able to confirm or deny information that you may already have, however, information such as insurance information, report numbers, personal details regarding those involved in the crash, etc. will not be released.

facts.claim: Under Michigan's FOIA policy, all persons except those incarcerated in state or local correctional facilities are entitled to information about the affairs of government.
facts.quote: It is the public policy of this state that all persons, except those persons incarcerated in state or local correctional facilities, are entitled to full and complete information regarding the affairs of government

facts.claim: By law, all law enforcement agencies must submit qualifying crash reports (UD-10) to the MSP.
facts.quote: By law, all law enforcement agencies are required to submit qualifying crash reports (UD-10) to the MSP.

facts.claim: The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit cannot change a report, and all changes must be raised with the law enforcement agency that reported the crash.
facts.quote: The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit cannot make changes to the report. All changes must be addressed with the law enforcement agency that reported the crash.

facts.claim: For a report number, insurance information or involved-party information, the Traffic Crash Reporting Unit directs people to the law enforcement agency that responded and reported the incident.
facts.quote: If you are in need of this information, please contact the Law Enforcement Agency that responded and reported the incident.

facts.claim: The MSP says MCL 257.622 requires the driver in a crash that injures or kills any person, or causes apparent property damage totaling $1,000.00 or more, to report it immediately.
facts.quote: MCL 257.622 states that the driver of a motor vehicle involved in an accident that injures or kills any person, or that damages property to an apparent extent totaling $1,000.00 or more, shall immediately report that accident

facts.claim: To file a UD-10 Traffic Crash Report, contact a law enforcement agency in your area or a Michigan State Police post.
facts.quote: To file a Traffic Crash Report (UD-10), please contact a law enforcement agency in your area or a Michigan State Police Post.

facts.claim: The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit cannot file a crash report for you.
facts.quote: The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit CANNOT file a report for you.

facts.claim: For a crash that was not reported immediately, the reporting agency decides whether a report will be filed.
facts.quote: Crashes that are not reported immediately are subject to the discretion of the reporting agency if a report will be filed for the crash.

facts.claim: TCPS purchase receipts are available by logging in to the same MiLogin account used for the purchase on the TCPS website (www.michigan.gov/tcps).
facts.quote: Receipts for purchases made within the Traffic Crash Purchasing System can be accessed by logging into the same MiLogin account that was used to make the purchase on the TCPS website (www.michigan.gov/tcps).

facts.claim: The MSP says all reported traffic crashes appear on your driving record, regardless of fault.
facts.quote: Please note all reported traffic crashes will appear on your driving record, regardless of fault in the accident

facts.claim: To find a report in TCPS you need either a driver license number or the case/incident number, plus a date of birth and the date of the crash, both of which are required.
facts.quote: Crash Report Search Requirements: Driver License Number or Case/Incident Number Date of Birth - required. Date of Crash - required.

facts.claim: You need a MiLogin account to use TCPS; if you don't have one, you must register first, and after registering you are taken to the TCPS site automatically.
facts.quote: If you do not have a MiLogin account, you must first register before you can access TCPS. Upon successful registration, you will be automatically directed to the TCPS site.

facts.claim: Paying an MSP records-request fee online, in the portal or the online payment center, adds a $2.00 processing fee; payment by check or money order made payable to the State of Michigan carries no fee.
facts.quote: Please note there is a $2.00 processing fee for online payments. Payments are accepted at no fee by check or money order, made payable to the State of Michigan.

facts.claim: If you don't have the information TCPS requires to search for a report, the MSP advises submitting a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request instead.
facts.quote: Users that do not have the required information are advised to submit a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request.

facts.claim: Mailed MSP records requests go to Michigan State Police, Records Resource Section, P.O. Box 30634, Lansing, Michigan 48909; overnight mail goes to 7150 Harris Drive, Dimondale, Michigan 48821.
facts.quote: Standard mail can be sent to Michigan State Police, Records Resource Section, P.O. Box 30634, Lansing, Michigan 48909. Overnight mail can be sent to Michigan State Police, Records Resource Section, 7150 Harris Drive, Dimondale, Michigan 48821.

facts.claim: Besides the online portal, MSP records requests can be emailed to MSPRecords@Michigan.gov, faxed to 517-241-1935, or mailed to Michigan State Police, Records Resource Section, P.O. Box 30634, Lansing, MI 48909.
facts.quote: Email MSPRecords@Michigan.gov Fax 517-241-1935 Mail Michigan State Police Records Resource Section P.O. Box 30634 Lansing, MI 48909

facts.claim: MSP records requests can be handed in at the security desk in the lobby of MSP Headquarters, 7150 Harris Drive, Dimondale, Michigan 48821, or at any Michigan State Police post.
facts.quote: Our physical address is 7150 Harris Drive, Dimondale, Michigan 48821. Requests may be submitted at the security desk in the lobby or at any Michigan State Police Post.

facts.claim: The MSP does not offer same-day service on records requests, and only the Records Resource Section can release records.
facts.quote: Please be advised, the MSP does not offer same day service and records cannot be released by worksites other than the Records Resource Section.

facts.claim: The MSP asks people not to submit the same records request by more than one method.
facts.quote: You can use the Request for Public Records Form as a template for your request, but it is not required. Please do not submit your request by multiple methods.

facts.claim: The MSP cannot estimate a records-request fee until it receives the request, and then tells you whether a payment or good-faith deposit is needed.

facts.claim: Any fee for an MSP records request must be paid before the MSP produces the documents.

facts.claim: Check or money order payments for MSP records requests can take up to 5 business days to process; include the request number (CR) from the letter's subject line, or a copy of the letter, with the payment.
facts.quote: Payments made by check or money order may take up to 5 business days to process. To ensure proper credit, please include your request number (CR), which is found in the subject line of the letter, with your payment or include a copy of the letter.

facts.claim: The MSP's Affidavit of Indigency is form DIR-103, and the indigency waiver is subject to the terms of the FOIA.
facts.quote: For requestors that meet the indigency criteria, you may submit an DIR-103 Affidavit of Indigency along with your request. If you qualify, the first $20 of the fee will be waived. The indigent waiver is subject to the terms in the FOIA.

facts.claim: Responses to portal requests are posted in the portal for download, while responses to email, fax or mail requests are sent by U.S. mail.

facts.claim: Most MSP records cannot be sent by email or fax because of security and privacy policies.
facts.quote: Most MSP documents cannot be emailed or faxed due to security policies and privacy concerns.

facts.claim: The MSP Records Resource Section can be reached at MSPRecords@michigan.gov or 517-241-1934.
facts.quote: The Records Resource Section can be contacted at MSPRecords@michigan.gov. Alternatively, you may call 517-241-1934.

facts.claim: The MSP Public Records Request Portal can only be reached through MiLogin, and a MiLogin account is free to create.
facts.quote: The Michigan State Police (MSP) Public Records Request Portal can only be accessed through the MiLogin website. A MiLogin account is free to create and provides you with access to a variety of State of Michigan applications.

facts.claim: A records request made through the MSP portal must include the requester's first name, last name, email and address.
facts.quote: Requestors must provide their first name, last name, email, and address.

facts.claim: Reports bought on the old TCPS appear in MiLogin only if you register for MiLogin with the same email address.
facts.quote: Purchases made within the previous TCPS will appear in MiLogin only if the same email address is used for the new MiLogin registration.

facts.claim: Searching for TCPS under 'Discover Online Services' in the MiLogin portal will not find it and returns a 'No service found' error.

facts.claim: For MiLogin account questions, the MSP's TCPS page points users to the DTMB Client Service Center at 517-241-9700 or 1-800-968-2644.
facts.quote: contact the DTMB Client Service Center at 517-241-9700 or 1-800-968-2644 if you have any questions.

facts.claim: The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit will not give out a report's incident/case number.
facts.quote: The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit will not provide you with the report incident/case number.

facts.claim: The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit will not provide information from a crash report by phone, mail, email or fax.
facts.quote: The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit will not provide you with information from the Traffic Crash Report via phone, mail, email or fax.

facts.claim: Whether a report is changed, and whether an update is sent to the MSP, is up to the reporting agency, whose name appears at the top of the UD-10 under 'Department Name'.

facts.claim: The MSP directs driving-record questions to the Michigan Department of Secretary of State Office, Driving Records Activity Unit, at 517-636-6406.

gaps.reason: The TCPS portal (michigan.gov/tcps, which redirects to tcps.state.mi.us) returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so no official page confirmed whether a card or convenience fee is added to the $15.00 TCPS price, or which payment methods are accepted. The law or rule that sets the $15 fee could not be read either: the House Fiscal Agency PDF (house.mi.gov) was unreachable and legislature.mi.gov returned 403.
The TCPS portal itself could not be opened (HTTP 403), so the purchase steps are confirmed only from MSP information pages.

MSP pages conflict. The Traffic Crash Reporting Unit FAQ says online purchase through TCPS is 'the only way to obtain a traffic crash report', while the MSP FOIA FAQ says you can instead use the Public Records Request Portal, email, fax or mail. No official mailing address, email or fax number for sending a crash report request was found; the only mailing address found is the Cashier's Unit address for payments.
No official source describes requesting a crash report in person from the MSP. The only in-person option found is picking up FOIA responses at MSP Headquarters in Dimondale with advance notice.

No official MSP page states an eligibility restriction or confidentiality period for buying a crash report through TCPS. The pages give only example account types and the required search details. The relevant statute text at legislature.mi.gov could not be opened (HTTP 403).

State pages say all agencies submit UD-10s to the MSP and TCPS sells reports from all Michigan agencies. It was not confirmed from a state source whether city police departments or county sheriffs also sell reports themselves or through vendor portals such as LexisNexis BuyCrash. Local agency pages are outside the allowed source list, and the web search budget ran out before more could be checked.

The MCL 257.622 reporting duty is quoted from the MSP FAQ's summary because the statute page on legislature.mi.gov returned HTTP 403. No official source describes a separate state form drivers must file themselves; the MSP says to report crashes to a law enforcement agency or MSP post.
A secondary search summary said each MSP post retains crash reports for the current year plus two years. This could not be found on any official page and is not included.

facts.claim: Minnesota Department of Public Safety, Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) says it maintains crash records under state and federal law.
facts.quote: Crash records, driving records, and motor vehicle records are maintained in accordance with State and Federal laws.

facts.claim: Minnesota law requires a peace officer who investigates a reportable crash in the regular course of duty to submit a report of it to the commissioner of public safety within ten days after the crash.
facts.quote: A peace officer who investigates in the regular course of duty an accident that is required to be reported under this section must submit an electronic or written report of the accident to the commissioner of public safety within ten days after the date of the accident.

facts.claim: Under Minnesota Statutes section 169.09, crashes on streets, highways and other parts of a public right-of-way must be reported if they result in one of the outcomes the statute lists.
facts.quote: Accidents on streets, highways, roadways, sidewalks, shoulders, shared use paths, or any other portion of a public right-of-way must be reported under the requirements of this section if the accident results in:

facts.claim: One listed outcome that makes a crash reportable is bodily injury where the person immediately receives medical treatment, at the scene or away from it.
facts.quote: (2) bodily injury to a person who, because of the injury, immediately receives medical treatment away from or at the scene of the accident;

facts.claim: Another listed outcome is disabling damage that requires a vehicle to be towed or otherwise transported from the scene.
facts.quote: (3) one or more of the motor vehicles incurring disabling damage that requires a vehicle to be transported away from the scene of the accident by tow truck or other vehicle; or

facts.claim: Damage to fixtures, infrastructure or other property alongside or on a highway also makes a crash reportable.
facts.quote: (4) damage to fixtures, infrastructure, or any other property alongside or on a highway.

facts.claim: DPS says crash reports can be obtained in person at DVS or from a full-service deputy registrar office.
facts.quote: Crash reports can be obtained in person at DVS or from a full-service deputy registrar office.

facts.claim: To request a report, you complete the Crash Record Request Form (PS2503) and submit it in person, at a full-service deputy registrar office, or by mail.
facts.quote: Complete a Crash Record Request Form (PS2503) and submit it in person, at a full-service deputy registrar office or by mail.

facts.claim: The DPS in-person location is the Driver and Vehicle Services Downtown Saint Paul Exam Station in the Town Square Building, 445 Minnesota St., St. Paul, MN 55101-5190.
facts.quote: Driver and Vehicle Services - Downtown Saint Paul Exam Station Town Square Building (street level) 445 Minnesota St. St. Paul, MN 55101-5190

facts.claim: The DPS crash report page links to a locator for full-service deputy registrar offices.
facts.quote: Find a full-service deputy registrar office near you.

facts.claim: Mail requests go to Driver and Vehicle Services, Attn: Records Unit, 445 Minnesota St., Suite 161, St. Paul, MN 55101-5161.
facts.quote: Driver and Vehicle Services Attn: Records Unit 445 Minnesota St., Suite 161 St. Paul, MN 55101-5161

facts.claim: The PS2503 form says checks and money orders should be made payable to DVS.
facts.quote: Checks/money orders should be made payable to DVS.

facts.claim: A request will not be processed without a signature from an authorized requester.
facts.quote: Requests will not be processed without a signature from an authorized requester.

facts.claim: In the office, the requester must present a driver's license, a government-issued identification card or a notarized signature.
facts.quote: Identification required in office: Requester must present driver's license, government-issued identification card or notarized signature.

facts.claim: By mail, the requester must include a legible copy of a driver's license or government-issued identification card, or a notarized signature.
facts.quote: Identification required by mail: Requester must include legible copy of driver's license, government-issued identification card or notarized signature.

facts.claim: The form asks you to complete all known crash fields, and a request cannot be completed if too little crash information is given.
facts.quote: Please complete all known fields. If insufficient crash information is provided, the request cannot be completed.

facts.claim: The crash information on the form includes the law enforcement case number, crash location, county and date of the crash.
facts.quote: Law enforcement case # Location of crash (street or highway) County Date of crash (mm/dd/yyyy)

facts.claim: The form asks for the names of up to two people involved in the crash.
facts.quote: Person 1 involved (last name, first, middle) Person 2 involved (last name, first, middle)

facts.claim: For each person involved, the form also asks for a driver's license number, license state and date of birth.
facts.quote: Driver's license # DL state Date of birth

facts.claim: In a fatal crash, the next of kin or legal representative must provide proof of death, such as a death certificate, obituary or memorial card.
facts.quote: Please note: in the case of a fatality, the next of kin or legal rep. must provide proof of death: death certificate, obituary or memorial card.

facts.claim: DPS says a crash report costs $5.
facts.quote: A crash report costs $5.

facts.claim: The PS2503 form says a $5.00 fee is due for each requested copy.
facts.quote: $5.00 fee is due for each requested copy.

facts.claim: State law sets the $5 fee that the commissioner of public safety or a full-service provider must charge authorized persons for a copy of a crash report.
facts.quote: The commissioner of public safety or full-service provider as defined in section 171.01, subdivision 33a, must charge authorized persons as described in paragraph (a) a $5 fee for a copy of an accident report.

facts.claim: DPS says crash reports are available three weeks after the incident.
facts.quote: Reports are available three weeks after the incident.

facts.claim: DPS says crash reports are only available to the people involved in the crash or their authorized agent.
facts.quote: They are only available to the individuals involved in the crash or their authorized agent.

facts.claim: An authorized requestor is a person involved in the crash who is recorded on the police report, such as a driver, passenger, pedestrian, vehicle owner or owner of damaged property.
facts.quote: An authorized requestor is a person involved with the crash (such as driver, passenger, owner of damaged property, owner of vehicle or pedestrian) who is recorded on the police report.

facts.claim: An authorized agent such as an insurance company or attorney may get a copy with a signed release from a party involved in the crash.
facts.quote: An authorized agent, such as an insurance company or an attorney, may obtain a copy of a crash report with a signed release from a party involved in the crash.

facts.claim: After a fatal crash, the next of kin, surviving spouse or legal representative of the estate must provide proof of death to get the report.
facts.quote: In the case of a fatality, the next of kin, surviving spouse or legal representative of the estate must provide proof of death such as a death certificate, obituary or memorial card.

facts.claim: By statute, the report must be disclosed on written request to anyone involved in the crash, the representative of their estate, a surviving spouse, surviving next of kin, or a trustee appointed under section 573.02.
facts.quote: (i) any individual involved in the accident, the representative of the individual's estate, or the surviving spouse, or one or more surviving next of kin, or a trustee appointed under section 573.02;

facts.claim: The statute also allows disclosure to anyone injured in person, property or means of support, or who suffers other financial loss because of the crash.
facts.quote: (ii) any other person injured in person, property, or means of support, or who incurs other pecuniary loss by virtue of the accident;

facts.claim: Legal counsel for those people may also get the report.
facts.quote: (iii) legal counsel of a person described in item (i) or (ii);

facts.claim: A representative of the insurer of those people may also get the report.
facts.quote: (iv) a representative of the insurer of any person described in item (i) or (ii); or

facts.claim: DPS says all crash reports are confidential and cannot be used as evidence in a civil or criminal trial.
facts.quote: All crash reports are confidential. They cannot be used as evidence in trial (civil or criminal)

facts.claim: State law says a crash report must not be used as evidence in any civil or criminal trial or damages action arising from the crash.
facts.quote: A report must not be used as evidence in any trial, civil or criminal, or any action for damages or criminal proceedings arising out of an accident.

facts.claim: Disclosing information from a crash report except as the law allows is a misdemeanor.
facts.quote: Disclosing any information contained in any accident report, except as provided in this subdivision, section 13.82, subdivision 3 or 6, or other statutes, is a misdemeanor.

facts.claim: State law says that, on written request, DPS, a full-service provider or any law enforcement agency must disclose the officer's crash report to the people the statute lists.
facts.quote: upon written request, the commissioner of public safety, a full-service provider as defined in section 171.01, subdivision 33a, or any law enforcement agency must disclose the report required under subdivision 8 to:

facts.claim: For example, the City of Minneapolis says people in a car crash in Minneapolis can request a copy of the accident report from the city.
facts.quote: If you are in a car accident in Minneapolis, you can request a copy of the accident report.

facts.claim: Minneapolis says it does not charge for individual accident reports.
facts.quote: We do not charge for individual accident reports.

facts.claim: DPS says crash reports are no longer submitted to DVS, because Minnesota Statutes section 169.09, subdivision 7 was repealed effective July 1, 2021.
facts.quote: Reports are no longer submitted to Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS). Minnesota Statutes, section 169.09, subdivision 7 was repealed effective July 1, 2021.

facts.quote: 2021 Subd. 7 Repealed 2021 c 5 art 4 s 151

facts.claim: That notice goes to the local police department within a city, to a State Patrol officer on a trunk highway, or otherwise to the county sheriff's office.
facts.quote: give notice of the collision to the local police department if the collision occurs within a municipality, to a State Patrol officer if the collision occurs on a trunk highway, or to the office of the sheriff of the county.

facts.quote: Step 1: Complete an accident request form Step 2: Submit the request online

facts.claim: A driver in a crash that injures or kills another person must, after meeting the statute's stop-and-information duties, notify law enforcement of the crash by the quickest means of communication.
facts.quote: The driver of a vehicle involved in a collision resulting in bodily injury to or death of another shall, after compliance with this section and by the quickest means of communication, give notice of the collision

facts.claim: The first outcome on the statute's list of reportable crashes is a fatality.
facts.quote: (1) a fatality;

facts.claim: Crashes on public lands or trail systems that have one of the listed outcomes must also be reported.
facts.quote: Accidents occurring on public lands or trail systems that result in the circumstances specified in paragraph (b) must be reported under the requirements of this section.

facts.claim: The statute defines disabling damage as damage that keeps a vehicle from leaving the scene in its usual manner in daylight after simple repairs.
facts.quote: For purposes of this section, "disabling damage" means damage that prevents a motor vehicle from departing the scene of the accident in its usual manner in daylight after simple repairs.

facts.claim: Crash reports and the data in them are not discoverable under any law or court rule.
facts.quote: Accident reports and data contained in the reports are not discoverable under any provision of law or rule of court.

facts.quote: It is intended by this subdivision to render privileged the reports required, but it is not intended to prohibit proof of the facts to which the reports relate.

facts.claim: The authorized-requester boxes on form PS2503 are driver, passenger, pedestrian, next of kin, owner of damaged property, owner of vehicle, parent/guardian, insurance representative and legal representative. The last two also give the client's name.
facts.quote: Check one box for authorized requester: Driver Passenger Pedestrian Next of kin Owner of damaged property Owner of vehicle Parent/guardian Insurance representative - Client name: Legal representative - Client name:

facts.quote: The driver of a vehicle involved in an accident resulting in bodily injury to or death of any individual or total property damage to an apparent extent of $1,000 or more, shall forward a written report of the accident to the commissioner of public safety within ten days of the accident.

facts.claim: Minneapolis says a person who was in the accident, or their lawyer or insurance company, may request the accident report.
facts.quote: The following people may request an accident report: A person who was in the accident (or their lawyer or insurance company)

facts.quote: When you request a complete report, you will need to show proof of your identity and role. Your request cannot be processed without the accompanying proof of identity or authorization.

facts.quote: Electronically: Go to the Open City Portal and select the link to "Accident Reports." Attach this or another authorization form, copies of ID and required documents to the request as you submit it.

facts.claim: The 'Accident Reports' request on Minneapolis's OpenCity Portal does not require registration.
